newsitem.title: USA: US BLS's Abraham has no firm estimate of CPI bias.
newsitem.headline: US BLS's Abraham has no firm estimate of CPI bias.

text.p: Katharine Abraham, commissioner of the Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics, on Tuesday said she had no firm estimate of the extent to which the Consumer Price Index overstates increases in the cost of living.
"I don't have an estimate of the bias," Abraham said at a briefing for reporters.
She pointed out that the monthly index, which measures the prices changes of a fixed basket of goods, is not a true cost-of-living measure, although it attempts to approximate one.

Because the fixed market basket cannot capture consumers' tendency to substitute to a different item when the price of one item goes up -- such as substituting chicken for steak -- Abraham said it tends to overstate cost of living.
"There is an upward bias in that the CPI does not allow for substitution in what people are buying," she said, but said she could not quantify the bias.
The briefing was held one day before a congressionally appointed commission was scheduled to release a report looking at perceived inaccuracies in the CPI.
The commission, headed by Stanford University economist Michael Boskin, is expected to conclude in the report that the index overstates inflation by a percentage point or more a year.
In addition to the substitution bias, many economists, including Abraham, have pointed to the difficulty of incorporating new products into the index on a timely basis.
Abraham said that would be one of the most difficult issues to resolve in any effort to improve the CPI.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics official listed a series of steps the agency has planned for the near future aimed at improving the CPI.

Those include the regular 10-year updating of the market basket, which will become effective with the release of data for January 1998. Abraham estimated that change would reduce measured inflation by 0.1 to 0.2 percentage point a year.

Starting in early 1997, the bureau will also begin publishing an experimental index, called the "geometric mean," which aims to take account of substitution of items within various categories of the index. For example, consumers might buy Gala apples instead of Fuji apples when the price of Galas declines.
At the start of this year, the bureau will also change the way it calculates medical care costs to try to provide a more accurate picture of price changes.
